title: Inorganic Chemistry: Advanced Topics
description: Symmetry and group theory, ligand field theory, coordination chemistry, organometallic catalysis, main-group and solid-state chemistry, redox diagrams and bioinorganic chemistry.

entries.name: Symmetry elements and point groups
entries.tagline: Classifying molecules by their symmetry, the starting point for group theory.

facts: A proper rotation by 360°/n about an axis.
A mirror plane. σₕ is perpendicular to the principal axis, σᵥ contains it, and σ_d bisects the angle between C₂ axes.
A center of inversion: every point (x, y, z) goes to (−x, −y, −z).
An improper rotation: a rotation by 360°/n followed by reflection in the plane perpendicular to the axis. S₁ = σ and S₂ = i.

points: Linear: D∞h if there is a center of inversion (CO₂, H₂), otherwise C∞v (HCl, CO).
Very high symmetry: T_d (tetrahedral, CH₄), O_h (octahedral, SF₆), I_h (icosahedral, C₆₀).
Otherwise find the highest-order rotation axis Cₙ. Then look for n perpendicular C₂ axes (the D groups), and for a σₕ (adds h), or σᵥ planes (adds v), or an S₂ₙ axis.
Examples: H₂O is C₂ᵥ, NH₃ is C₃ᵥ, BF₃ is D₃ₕ, trans-N₂F₂ is C₂ₕ, benzene is D₆ₕ, and staggered ethane is D₃d.
A molecule can be chiral only if it has no improper axis (no mirror plane, no inversion center and no Sₙ).
A molecule can have a permanent dipole moment only if it belongs to C₁, Cₛ or Cₙ or Cₙᵥ.
The point group decides which vibrations are IR or Raman active, how orbitals can combine, and which electronic transitions are allowed.

sections.text: Each point group has a character table. Its rows are irreducible representations, the symmetry types that orbitals and vibrations can have, and its columns are classes of operations. Mulliken symbols: A and B are singly degenerate (A symmetric and B antisymmetric about the principal axis), E is doubly degenerate and T triply degenerate. The subscripts g and u (even and odd under inversion) and numbers 1, 2 distinguish the types. Columns on the right show which representation x, y, z, rotations and quadratic functions transform as.

quiz.q: What is the point group of water?
What is the point group of ammonia?

entries.name: Group theory applications: vibrations and orbitals
entries.tagline: Using symmetry to find the vibrations of a molecule and to build its molecular orbitals.

points: Determine the point group and write down the operations.

Build the reducible representation of all 3N Cartesian displacements: for each operation, count the atoms left in place (unshifted atoms), multiply by the character of that operation for one atom (E: 3, C₂: −1, σ: 1, i: −3, C₃: 0, and so on).
Reduce it with the formula n(Γᵢ) = (1/h) Σ χ(R) χᵢ(R), where h is the order of the group.
Subtract the representations of the three translations (x, y, z) and three rotations (or two for linear molecules). What is left is Γ_vib.
A mode is IR active if it transforms as x, y or z, and Raman active if it transforms as a quadratic function (x², xy, and so on).

facts: Γ_vib = 2A₁ + B₁. All three modes are both IR and Raman active.
Σg⁺ (symmetric stretch, Raman only), Πu (bend, IR only) and Σu⁺ (asymmetric stretch, IR only). Consistent with mutual exclusion.
Γ_vib = A₁g + E_g + 2T₁u + T₂g + T₂u. Only the two T₁u modes are IR active, and A₁g, E_g and T₂g are Raman active. The T₂u mode is silent in both.

sections.text: Group the ligand orbitals into symmetry-adapted linear combinations (SALCs), each of which transforms as one irreducible representation. Only orbitals of the same symmetry can interact. For water, the two H 1s orbitals give SALCs of a₁ and b₂ symmetry. The oxygen 2s and 2pz are a₁, 2px is b₁ and 2py is b₂. So the a₁ and b₂ SALCs combine with the oxygen a₁ and b₂ orbitals, while the 2px (b₁) is left nonbonding. A projection operator generates SALCs from the characters.

quiz.q: For which vibrational modes in CO₂ is the mutual exclusion rule illustrated?
quiz.a: The modes that are IR active are Raman inactive, and the reverse
wrong: All modes are both IR and Raman active
None of the modes is active

entries.name: Molecular orbitals of polyatomic molecules
entries.tagline: From water to hypervalent compounds: what MO theory says that Lewis structures cannot.

points: Eight valence electrons fill the orbitals 2a₁ (mostly O 2s), 1b₂ (bonding), 3a₁ (mostly bonding with some lone-pair character) and 1b₁ (a nonbonding oxygen 2p, the HOMO).

The two highest filled orbitals are different in energy and in type. Photoelectron spectroscopy shows two different ionization energies, which contradicts the simple picture of two equivalent 'rabbit-ear' lone pairs. The orbital picture is the one supported by experiment.

sections.text: A Walsh diagram plots orbital energies against bond angle. It explains the geometries of AH₂ molecules. With 4 valence electrons (BeH₂) the molecule is linear. With 8 (H₂O) it is bent, because the 3a₁ orbital drops in energy on bending, since the oxygen 2s mixes in more with the 2p. Similar diagrams explain the shapes of AB₂ molecules for different electron counts.

points: A three-center two-electron (3c-2e) bond uses one pair of electrons to hold three atoms. It occurs in the bridging hydrogens of diborane, B₂H₆.

A three-center four-electron (3c-4e) bond explains hypervalent molecules such as SF₆, XeF₂ and I₃⁻ without needing d orbitals. Three p orbitals give a bonding, a nonbonding and an antibonding combination. Four electrons fill the first two, so the outer atoms carry negative charge and the bonding is mostly ionic.
Calculations show that d-orbital participation in the main-group elements is minor.

sections.text: The HOMO and LUMO, the frontier orbitals, control reactivity and spectra: nucleophiles use the HOMO and electrophiles the LUMO.

quiz.q: What explains the bonding in hypervalent molecules such as SF₆ without needing d orbitals?

entries.name: Ligand field theory: geometry, LFSE and Jahn–Teller
entries.tagline: How the shape of a complex splits the d orbitals, and what this does to energies and magnetism.

points: The d orbitals split into t₂g (dxy, dxz, dyz), at −0.4Δₒ, and e_g (dz², dx²−y²), at +0.6Δₒ.
LFSE = (−0.4 n(t₂g) + 0.6 n(e_g)) Δₒ, plus the pairing energy P for each extra pair formed.

For d⁴ to d⁷, there is a choice. If Δₒ < P the electrons spread out (high spin), and if Δₒ > P they pair (low spin). Weak-field ligands (halides, H₂O) usually give high spin and strong-field ligands (CN⁻, CO) give low spin. For d¹–d³ and d⁸–d¹⁰ there is no choice.
Δₒ increases down a group (3d < 4d < 5d), so 4d and 5d complexes are nearly always low spin, and it increases with the oxidation state of the metal.

sections.text: Low-spin d⁶ (Co³⁺ with strong-field ligands): t₂g⁶ gives −2.4Δₒ, with the extra pairing energy of 2P. High-spin d⁶ (t₂g⁴ e_g²) gives −0.4 × 4 + 0.6 × 2 = −0.4Δₒ. So the low-spin complex has far greater stabilization.

The splitting is inverted (e below t₂) and small: Δₜ = (4/9)Δₒ. It is almost always smaller than the pairing energy, so tetrahedral complexes are nearly always high spin. Tetrahedral geometry is common for d⁰, d⁵ (high spin) and d¹⁰, which have no LFSE preference, and for large ligands such as Cl⁻.

The strongest splitting, with dx²−y² far above the others. Electronic configuration d⁸ with strong-field ligands places all eight electrons in the lower four orbitals, which gives a diamagnetic square planar complex. Examples: Pt(II), Pd(II), Au(III), Rh(I), Ir(I) and Ni(II) with CN⁻.

A non-linear molecule in a degenerate electronic state distorts to remove the degeneracy and lower the energy. In octahedral complexes the effect is strong when the e_g orbitals are unevenly occupied: high-spin d⁴ (Cr²⁺, Mn³⁺), low-spin d⁷ and d⁹ (Cu²⁺). Typically two trans bonds are longer, as in the elongated octahedra of Cu²⁺ complexes.
n is the number of unpaired electrons. High-spin d⁵ (n = 5) gives 5.92 BM, and low-spin d⁶ is 0 (diamagnetic).

quiz.q: Why are tetrahedral complexes almost always high spin?
quiz.a: Δₜ is small, only 4/9 of Δₒ, so less than the pairing energy

quiz.q: What is the spin-only magnetic moment for 3 unpaired electrons?

entries.name: Electronic spectra of complexes and Tanabe–Sugano diagrams
entries.tagline: Why complexes are colored, how intense the colors are, and how to read the spectrum.

sections.text: A d-electron configuration gives several terms (states) for the free ion, and the octahedral field splits them. For d¹ the ²D term splits into ²T₂g (ground) and ²E_g, giving one band. For d² the ground term is ³F (Hund) and it splits into ³T₁g, ³T₂g and ³A₂g, with the excited ³P term becoming ³T₁g(P).
Two spin-allowed bands: ν₁ (³T₁g → ³T₂g) at about 17 800 cm⁻¹ and ν₂ (³T₁g → ³T₁g(P)) at about 25 700 cm⁻¹. The ratio of the two energies gives Δₒ and the Racah parameter B.

These plot the energies of all the states (as E/B) against Δₒ/B for each d configuration. For d⁴ to d⁷ there is a crossing at the point where the ground state changes from high spin to low spin. They are used to assign spectra and to find Δₒ and B from the positions of the bands. An Orgel diagram is a simpler version for high-spin complexes.

points: Spin-forbidden bands (ΔS ≠ 0) are very weak. High-spin d⁵ complexes, such as Mn²⁺, have no spin-allowed d–d bands, so they are very pale (ε about 0.01–0.1).

The Laporte rule forbids d–d transitions in centrosymmetric complexes, so octahedral complexes are weakly colored (ε about 1–100). Vibrations that remove the inversion center (vibronic coupling) let them appear.
Tetrahedral complexes have no inversion center, so bands are 10–100 times stronger. [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is pale pink (ε about 10) and [CoCl₄]²⁻ a vivid blue (ε about 600).
Charge-transfer bands are fully allowed and intense (ε about 1000–50 000): ligand-to-metal (LMCT), such as the purple of MnO₄⁻, and metal-to-ligand (MLCT), such as in [Ru(bpy)₃]²⁺.

sections.text: The Racah parameter B (a measure of electron repulsion) is smaller in a complex than in the free ion, because the electrons spread out onto the ligands. The 'cloud-expanding' nephelauxetic effect shows covalency and increases along a series of ligands: F⁻ < H₂O < NH₃ < Cl⁻ < Br⁻ < I⁻.

quiz.q: Why are high-spin Mn²⁺ complexes very pale?
wrong: They absorb only in the UV

quiz.q: Why is [CoCl₄]²⁻ much more intensely colored than [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺?
quiz.a: Tetrahedral complexes have no inversion center, so the Laporte rule does not apply

entries.name: Magnetism of coordination compounds
entries.tagline: What a magnetic measurement tells you about unpaired electrons and the geometry of a complex.

facts: All paired electrons. Weakly repelled by a magnetic field.
Unpaired electrons. Attracted into the field, and the effect decreases as temperature rises (Curie law).
Spins on neighboring atoms align in the same direction below the Curie temperature (iron, cobalt, nickel).
Neighbors align in opposite directions below the Néel temperature, with no net moment (MnO).

sections.h: Spin-only moment and the real one
points: The spin-only value is μₛ = √(n(n + 2)) Bohr magnetons, from the number of unpaired electrons n. Values: n = 1, 1.73; n = 2, 2.83; n = 3, 3.87; n = 4, 4.90; n = 5, 5.92.
The effective moment is measured from the molar magnetic susceptibility: μ_eff = 2.828 √(χ_M T) in BM.
In complexes of the first row the orbital motion is largely quenched when the ground term is A or E (as in d³, high-spin d⁵ and d⁸), so the spin-only formula works well.

When the ground term is a T term (for example high-spin octahedral Co²⁺), there is an orbital contribution, and the moment is higher than the spin-only value. For high-spin octahedral Co²⁺, the spin-only value is 3.87 BM while the observed values are about 4.7–5.2 BM.
For the 4d and 5d metals and the lanthanides, spin–orbit coupling is large and the simple formula fails.

sections.text: For some d⁴ to d⁷ complexes, notably Fe(II) d⁶ with a ligand field close to the pairing energy, the high-spin and low-spin states are close in energy, so they can switch with temperature, pressure or light. It involves a change in magnetism, color and metal–ligand bond lengths, and is studied for molecular switches and memory devices.

The Gouy balance and Faraday method weigh a sample in a field. The Evans method uses the shift of an NMR signal in solution. A SQUID magnetometer is very sensitive and measures over a wide range of temperatures and fields.

quiz.q: What is the spin-only magnetic moment for 5 unpaired electrons?

entries.name: Substitution mechanisms and the trans effect
entries.tagline: How fast ligands swap, by what route, and how to plan the synthesis of cisplatin.

sections.text: Taube's definition: a complex is labile if it exchanges ligands within about a minute at room temperature, and inert if it is slower. This is kinetic, not thermodynamic, and a complex can be stable but labile.
points: Inert octahedral complexes are those with high ligand field stabilization: d³ (Cr³⁺) and low-spin d⁶ (Co³⁺, Fe²⁺ with CN⁻) and low-spin d⁸ in some cases.
Water exchange rates span 15 orders of magnitude: Cr³⁺ about 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹, and Cu²⁺ about 10⁸–10⁹ s⁻¹. Cu²⁺ is extremely labile because of the Jahn–Teller distortion and a single electron in e_g.

facts: The leaving group departs first (or leads), giving a five-coordinate intermediate. Rate nearly independent of the entering group. Typical for octahedral complexes.

The entering ligand binds first, giving a higher coordination number. Rate depends on the nature of the entering group. Typical for square planar complexes of d⁸ metals (Pt(II)), which are 16-electron and have space for a fifth ligand.
Entering and leaving groups exchange in a concerted way. The Eigen–Wilkins mechanism describes the pre-equilibrium formation of an outer-sphere ion pair followed by interchange.

sections.text: The rate law has two terms: rate = k₁[complex] + k₂[complex][Y]. The first term is a solvent-assisted path and the second a direct attack by Y. The activation entropy is negative, as expected for an associative step.

In square planar Pt(II) complexes, the ligand trans to a good trans-directing ligand is replaced fastest. Order (strong to weak): CN⁻, CO, C₂H₄ > PR₃, H⁻ > SCN⁻, I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > NH₃ > OH⁻ > H₂O. The trans influence is the equilibrium weakening of the bond trans to the ligand, and the trans effect is the kinetic one.
points: Cisplatin: [PtCl₄]²⁻ + NH₃ gives [PtCl₃(NH₃)]⁻. The second NH₃ goes cis to the first, because it replaces the Cl⁻ trans to a Cl⁻ (trans effect of Cl⁻ > NH₃), giving cis-[PtCl₂(NH₃)₂].
Transplatin is made the other way: start from [Pt(NH₃)₄]²⁺ and add Cl⁻. After the first Cl⁻ goes on, the second replaces the NH₃ trans to it, because Cl⁻ is a stronger trans director than NH₃.

quiz.q: Which mechanism is typical for substitution at square planar Pt(II) complexes?
Which of these complexes is the most inert?

entries.name: Isomerism, nomenclature and the chelate effect
entries.tagline: How to name a complex and the many ways in which the same formula can be arranged.

points: List the ligands first, in alphabetical order, then the metal, with its oxidation state in Roman numerals.
Numerical prefixes di, tri, tetra for simple ligands, and bis, tris for ligands that already contain such a prefix, such as ethylenediamine.
Anionic ligands end in -o (chloro, cyano, hydroxo). Neutral ones keep their names, except aqua (H₂O), ammine (NH₃), carbonyl (CO).
If the complex is an anion, the metal name ends in -ate: K₄[Fe(CN)₆] is potassium hexacyanoferrate(II). [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂ is pentaamminechlorocobalt(III) chloride.

facts: Ions inside and outside the sphere swap: [Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄ (gives sulfate ions in water) and [Co(NH₃)₅SO₄]Br (gives bromide ions).
Water inside or outside the coordination sphere, such as the three isomers of CrCl₃·6H₂O.
An ambidentate ligand binds through different atoms: nitro (–NO₂, N-bound) versus nitrito (–ONO, O-bound); thiocyanate N or S.
Ligands swapped between the metal centers of a salt with a complex cation and a complex anion.

points: Geometric: [MA₄B₂] octahedral complexes are cis or trans. [MA₃B₃] is fac (the three A on one face) or mer (meridional, in a plane through the metal). Square planar [MA₂B₂] is cis or trans.
Optical: octahedral complexes with chelates, such as [Co(en)₃]³⁺, are chiral, as two propeller-like forms, Δ and Λ, that are mirror images.

sections.text: A ligand that binds through two or more donor atoms (denticity 2 or more: bidentate, such as ethylenediamine (en), and polydentate, such as EDTA) forms much more stable complexes than the same number of single-donor ligands. The reason is mainly entropy: replacing six ammonia molecules by three en molecules releases more free molecules, so ΔS is more positive. [Ni(en)₃]²⁺ is about 10¹⁰ times more stable than [Ni(NH₃)₆]²⁺.

quiz.q: How many geometric isomers does an octahedral complex of the type [MA₄B₂] have?
What mainly explains the chelate effect?

entries.name: Stability constants, the Irving–Williams series and HSAB
terms: hard and soft acids and bases
entries.tagline: How strongly metals bind ligands, and a rule of thumb for predicting who binds whom.

sections.text: For M + L ⇌ ML the stepwise constant is K₁ = [ML]/([M][L]). The overall constant β_n multiplies the stepwise ones. Successive constants usually decrease, K₁ > K₂ > K₃, for statistical reasons. A large β means a stable complex. They are measured by potentiometric, spectrophotometric or NMR titration.

For high-spin octahedral complexes of the divalent 3d metals, the stability increases across the series regardless of the ligand: Mn²⁺ < Fe²⁺ < Co²⁺ < Ni²⁺ < Cu²⁺ > Zn²⁺. It follows the decrease in ionic radius and the growth of ligand field stabilization, with a peak at Cu²⁺, where the Jahn–Teller effect adds more stabilization.

sections.h: Hard and soft acids and bases (Pearson)
facts: Small, highly charged, not very polarizable: H⁺, Li⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺, Fe³⁺, Cr³⁺, Ti⁴⁺.
Large, low charge, polarizable: Ag⁺, Cu⁺, Hg²⁺, Pd²⁺, Pt²⁺, Cd²⁺.
Small, not polarizable, with the donor atom of high electronegativity: F⁻, OH⁻, H₂O, NH₃, O-donors.
Large and polarizable: I⁻, S-donors (R₂S, thiolates), CN⁻, phosphines, CO.

sections.text: The principle: hard acids prefer hard bases and soft acids prefer soft bases. It is a rule of thumb for stability and reactivity.
points: Hg²⁺ binds sulfur very strongly, which is why mercury is found as cinnabar (HgS) and why it is toxic to enzymes with thiol groups.
Goldschmidt's geochemical classes follow it: hard metals (Al, Mg, Ca, Fe³⁺) in oxides and silicates, soft metals (Cu, Zn, Pb, Hg, Ag) in sulfides.
Thiocyanate (SCN⁻) is ambidentate: it binds through N to hard Fe³⁺ and through S to soft Pd²⁺.

quiz.q: Which divalent 3d metal forms the most stable complexes in the Irving–Williams series?
According to HSAB, which base prefers to bind Hg²⁺?

entries.name: The 18-electron rule and ligand types
entries.tagline: Counting electrons predicts which organometallic complexes are stable.

sections.text: A transition metal has nine valence orbitals (five d, one s, three p), which hold 18 electrons. Complexes that reach an 18-electron count, with all the bonding and nonbonding orbitals filled, are usually the most stable, especially with strong-field π-acceptor ligands.
Count the electrons of the neutral metal (its group number), add those donated by each ligand, and adjust for the overall charge. A metal–metal bond adds one electron to each metal.

points: Mn₂(CO)₁₀: each Mn has 7 + 5 × 2 + 1 (from the Mn–Mn bond) = 18.
Ferrocene, Fe(η⁵-C₅H₅)₂: 8 + 2 × 5 = 18.
Exceptions: square planar 16-electron complexes of d⁸ metals (Pd(II), Pt(II), Rh(I), Ir(I), such as Wilkinson's catalyst RhCl(PPh₃)₃), and early-metal complexes that do not reach 18.

sections.text: In the Dewar–Chatt–Duncanson model, CO donates a lone pair from carbon to the metal (σ donation) and the metal gives electrons from filled d orbitals into the empty π* orbitals of CO (back-donation, π-backbonding). The two effects reinforce each other, which makes CO a strong π-acceptor ligand.
points: Back-donation weakens the C–O bond, so the infrared stretch ν(CO) falls from 2143 cm⁻¹ in free CO: [Mn(CO)₆]⁺ 2090, Ni(CO)₄ 2060, Cr(CO)₆ 2000, [V(CO)₆]⁻ 1860 cm⁻¹. The more electron-rich the metal, the lower ν(CO).
Terminal CO is seen at about 1850–2125 cm⁻¹, bridging (μ₂) CO at about 1700–1850 cm⁻¹.

sections.text: PR₃ are σ-donors and weaker π-acceptors, and their properties are tuned through R. The Tolman cone angle measures their bulk: PMe₃ 118°, PPh₃ 145°, P(tBu)₃ 182°.

quiz.q: What is the electron count of Fe(CO)₅?
What happens to ν(CO) as the metal becomes more electron-rich?
quiz.a: It decreases, because back-donation is stronger

entries.name: Elementary steps in organometallic catalysis
entries.tagline: The handful of steps from which all homogeneous catalytic cycles are built.

facts: A ligand leaves (18 → 16 electrons) to open a site for the substrate, or binds (16 → 18). Catalysts need a vacant site.

A metal inserts into a bond A–B. The metal's oxidation state and electron count both go up by 2, and so does its coordination number. It needs a metal that is electron-rich and has a vacant site (typically d⁸ or d¹⁰, such as Ir(I) or Pd(0)). Substrates: H₂ (concerted), alkyl and aryl halides, HX. Example: Vaska's complex IrCl(CO)(PPh₃)₂ + H₂ → Ir(H)₂Cl(CO)(PPh₃)₂.
The reverse. Two cis ligands join and leave, forming a C–H, C–C or C–X bond. The oxidation state and electron count fall by 2. It is the product-forming step in many catalytic cycles.

A ligand moves onto an adjacent ligand: an alkyl group migrates onto a coordinated CO to form an acyl, or an alkene inserts into an M–H or M–C bond. The oxidation state does not change, and a vacant site is created.

An M–CH₂CH₂R alkyl loses a hydrogen from the β carbon to the metal, giving M–H and an alkene. It needs a vacant cis site and is the main reason metal alkyls with β hydrogens are unstable. The reverse is the insertion of an alkene into M–H.
A group transfers from one metal to another, such as from boron to palladium in the Suzuki reaction: Pd–X + R–B → Pd–R + X–B.

sections.text: In a catalytic cycle the metal complex is regenerated at the end of each turn. The turnover number (TON) is the moles of product per mole of catalyst before it dies, and the turnover frequency (TOF) is the TON per unit time. Good industrial catalysts reach TONs of 10⁵–10⁶ or more.

When drawing a cycle, track the oxidation state, the d electron count and the total electron count at each intermediate. They should change only by the amounts allowed in each step, and the catalyst should be back where it started.

quiz.q: In oxidative addition, what happens to the metal's oxidation state?
What does a metal alkyl need to undergo β-hydride elimination?
quiz.a: A β hydrogen and a vacant cis coordination site

entries.name: Industrial catalytic processes
entries.tagline: Hydrogenation, hydroformylation, acetic acid, the Wacker process, metathesis and polymerization, each seen as a cycle.

facts: A 16-electron Rh(I). PPh₃ dissociates, H₂ adds oxidatively, the alkene coordinates, inserts into Rh–H (migratory insertion), and the alkane leaves by reductive elimination.

Alkene + CO + H₂ → aldehyde, using HCo(CO)₄ or a rhodium phosphine catalyst. About 10 million tonnes a year of aldehydes, converted into alcohols and plasticizers. The ratio of linear to branched product is the key selectivity.

CH₃OH + CO → CH₃COOH with [Rh(CO)₂I₂]⁻. HI turns methanol into CH₃I, which adds oxidatively to Rh(I), the methyl migrates onto CO, giving an acyl, reductive elimination gives acetyl iodide, and hydrolysis gives acetic acid. The Cativa process (BP, 1996) uses iridium and is faster and cleaner.
Ethene + ½O₂ → acetaldehyde with PdCl₂ and CuCl₂. Water attacks coordinated ethene, β-hydride elimination follows, and the Pd(0) is reoxidized by Cu(II), which is reoxidized by oxygen.

Alkene double bonds are swapped, through a metal carbene and a metallacyclobutane (Chauvin mechanism, [2+2]). Grubbs (Ru) and Schrock (Mo) catalysts. Chauvin, Grubbs and Schrock shared the 2005 Nobel Prize.
Titanium catalysts with aluminium alkyls make polyethylene and stereoregular polypropylene by repeated insertion of the alkene into a Ti–C bond (Cossee–Arlman mechanism). Nobel Prize 1963.
Syngas (CO + H₂) over iron or cobalt gives hydrocarbons, a route from coal or gas to liquid fuels.

sections.text: Homogeneous catalysts (in solution) are more selective and easier to study, but harder to separate from the product. Heterogeneous catalysts (solids) are easy to separate and are used for large-scale processes.

quiz.q: What does the hydroformylation reaction make from an alkene, CO and H₂?
Which mechanism describes olefin metathesis?
quiz.a: The Chauvin mechanism, through a metallacyclobutane

entries.name: Metal–metal bonds and clusters
entries.tagline: Bonds directly between metal atoms, up to a quadruple bond.

sections.text: The d orbitals of two metal atoms can overlap to give sigma, pi and delta bonds. The octachlorodirhenate(III) ion, [Re₂Cl₈]²⁻, was recognized by F. A. Cotton in 1964 as having a quadruple bond.

points: Each Re(III) is d⁴, giving eight electrons to fill the bonding combinations σ² π⁴ δ², a bond order of 4.

The two ReCl₄ units are eclipsed (D₄ₕ), which you would not expect from steric effects alone. Eclipsing is needed for the two d_xy orbitals to overlap side-on in the δ bond. A twist of 45° would destroy it, so the structure is evidence for the bond.
Mn₂(CO)₁₀ has a single Mn–Mn bond (each Mn reaches 18 electrons).
Cr₂(OAc)₄(H₂O)₂ and Mo₂(OAc)₄ are paddlewheel compounds with quadruple bonds. Cr₂ complexes with extremely short bonds have been made.

Clusters such as Fe₃(CO)₁₂ and [Mo₆Cl₈]⁴⁺ have metal atoms held together in triangles and octahedra. Bonding in clusters is often counted with the cluster valence electron rules, similar to Wade's rules.

quiz.q: What is the bond order in [Re₂Cl₈]²⁻?

entries.name: Boranes and Wade's rules
entries.tagline: Cages of boron atoms bonded with fewer electron pairs than the atoms they hold together.

sections.text: Boron has three valence electrons but forms compounds with more bonds than it has electron pairs. Diborane, B₂H₆, has two terminal B–H bonds on each boron (ordinary 2c-2e bonds) and two bridging hydrogens that share B–H–B three-center two-electron bonds.

The shape of a borane cluster is predicted from the number of skeletal electron pairs. Each B–H unit contributes 2 skeletal electrons, each extra H contributes 1, and the charge is added. For n boron atoms:
facts: Closo (closed polyhedron). B₆H₆²⁻, an octahedron: 6 × 2 + 2 = 14 electrons, 7 pairs.
Nido (nest, a closo cage with one vertex missing). B₅H₉.

sections.text: Replacing BH⁻ by the isoelectronic CH gives carboranes, such as the icosahedral closo-C₂B₁₀H₁₂, which are very stable. Wade's rules also work for many metal clusters. William Lipscomb won the 1976 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work on borane structure and bonding.

quiz.q: How many skeletal electron pairs does a closo borane with n vertices have?

entries.name: Main-group compounds: silicates, silicones and noble gas chemistry
entries.tagline: Si–O frameworks, inorganic polymers and the compounds of the 'inert' gases.

sections.text: The Si–O bond is very strong (about 452 kJ/mol), so silicon is found in nature almost only as oxides and silicates, built from SiO₄ tetrahedra joined at the corners.
points: Isolated tetrahedra (olivine), chains (pyroxenes), double chains (amphiboles), sheets (micas, clays), and 3D frameworks (quartz, feldspars).

In aluminosilicates, some Si is replaced by Al, giving the framework a negative charge balanced by cations. Zeolites are aluminosilicates with open channels, used as molecular sieves, ion exchangers and catalysts.

sections.text: Polysiloxanes, (R₂SiO)ₙ, have a Si–O backbone with organic groups on silicon. They are thermally stable, flexible over a wide temperature range, water-repellent and chemically inert, so they are used for sealants, lubricants, medical implants and cookware.

Poly(dichlorophosphazene), (NPCl₂)ₙ, with an alternating P=N backbone, is made by heating (NPCl₂)₃. Replacing Cl by alkoxy or amino groups gives polymers with very different properties, from rubbers to biomedical materials.

Neil Bartlett made the first, Xe[PtF₆], in 1962, after noticing that PtF₆ ionizes O₂, and xenon has nearly the same ionization energy as O₂. Xenon fluorides are made from the elements: XeF₂ (linear), XeF₄ (square planar) and XeF₆ (distorted octahedral). They agree with VSEPR with lone pairs counted. They are strong fluorinating and oxidizing agents.
Compounds between halogens, such as ClF₃ (T-shaped), BrF₅ (square pyramidal) and IF₇ (pentagonal bipyramid), and ions such as I₃⁻ (linear). The larger halogen is the central atom.

quiz.q: What is the shape of XeF₄?
Why is silicon found almost only as silicates and oxides in nature?
quiz.a: The Si–O bond is very strong

entries.name: Ionic solid structures and the radius ratio
entries.tagline: Most ionic structures are close-packed anions with cations in the gaps.

sections.text: Spheres can be packed in layers in two ways: ABAB (hexagonal close packing, hcp) or ABCABC (cubic close packing, ccp, also called face-centered cubic). Both fill 74% of space. For N spheres there are N octahedral holes and 2N tetrahedral holes.

facts: Cl⁻ in ccp, Na⁺ in all the octahedral holes. Coordination 6:6. Also MgO, CaO, AgCl.
Simple cubic arrangement, 8:8. For a large cation.
S²⁻ in ccp, Zn²⁺ in half of the tetrahedral holes. 4:4. Wurtzite is the hcp version.
Ca²⁺ in ccp and F⁻ in all the tetrahedral holes. 8:4. Antifluorite (Li₂O) has the ions swapped.
The large A cation has 12-coordinate sites, and the small B cation 6-coordinate. The family includes ferroelectrics, high-temperature superconductors and solar cell materials.
Oxide in ccp, with A in tetrahedral and B in octahedral holes (normal), or the reverse (inverse).

sections.text: The coordination number is predicted from the ratio of cation to anion radius, r₊/r₋: 0.155–0.225 trigonal planar (3), 0.225–0.414 tetrahedral (4), 0.414–0.732 octahedral (6), 0.732–1.0 cubic (8). It is only a guide and has many exceptions, since ions are not hard spheres.
Close to 1 for the ideal cubic structure. Lower values give distorted structures.

quiz.q: In NaCl, which holes in the Cl⁻ lattice do the Na⁺ ions occupy?
What is the coordination number in the CsCl structure?

entries.name: Born–Haber cycle, lattice energy and defects
entries.tagline: How to measure lattice energy indirectly, how to calculate it, and what imperfections do.

sections.text: Hess's law is applied to the formation of an ionic solid from its elements. For NaCl, in kJ/mol:
equations: ΔH_f = ΔH_sub(Na) + ½D(Cl₂) + IE(Na) + EA(Cl) + U_lattice
sections.text: Every term except the lattice energy can be measured, so the cycle gives it.

The Born–Landé equation. M is the Madelung constant, which depends only on the crystal structure (1.748 for NaCl, 1.763 for CsCl, 1.638 for zinc blende), r₀ is the distance between the ions, and n the Born exponent that accounts for repulsion at short distance. The Kapustinskii equation estimates it from the formula, charges and radii alone. The lattice energy grows with the charges and with smaller ions.

facts: A missing cation and anion pair. The density falls. Common in NaCl and in compounds where cation and anion are similar in size.
An ion moves from its site into an interstitial site. Typical of AgCl, where the small Ag⁺ can fit in a gap.
Variable composition. Iron(II) oxide is Fe₀.₉₅O, with some Fe²⁺ replaced by Fe³⁺ and vacancies.
An electron trapped in an anion vacancy absorbs light. Heating NaCl in sodium vapor turns it yellow and KCl violet.

sections.text: Ions can hop through vacancies, so some solids conduct ions. Solid electrolytes such as β-alumina (Na⁺) and yttria-stabilized zirconia (O²⁻, used in solid oxide fuel cells) are used in batteries and sensors.

quiz.q: In the Born–Haber cycle for NaCl, what is the term that you solve for?
What is a Frenkel defect?
quiz.a: An ion displaced from its lattice site into an interstitial site
wrong: A missing cation and anion pair
An extra electron in the lattice
A foreign ion in the lattice

entries.name: Superconductivity and functional materials
entries.tagline: Materials that conduct electricity with no resistance, and why they matter.

sections.text: Below a critical temperature T_c, a superconductor has exactly zero electrical resistance and expels magnetic fields from its interior (the Meissner effect), which lets a magnet float above it. Heike Kamerlingh Onnes discovered it in 1911 in mercury, which becomes superconducting at 4.2 K.

In BCS theory (Bardeen, Cooper and Schrieffer, 1957) electrons form Cooper pairs through an attraction mediated by lattice vibrations (phonons). The pairs move through the lattice without scattering. It explains conventional superconductors, with T_c up to about 30–40 K.

points: Niobium–titanium and Nb₃Sn: the wires in MRI magnets and particle accelerators, cooled with liquid helium.
MgB₂: 39 K.

High-temperature cuprates: YBa₂Cu₃O₇ (YBCO), found in 1987, has T_c of 92 K, above the boiling point of liquid nitrogen (77 K), which makes cooling cheap. They are layered perovskite-like copper oxides. The mechanism is still debated.
Hydrides at very high pressure (hundreds of GPa) have been reported to superconduct at temperatures near room temperature.

sections.text: The properties of these materials depend on the exact oxygen content and doping, which is a matter of solid-state synthesis. YBa₂Cu₃O₇ made with less oxygen is not superconducting.

quiz.q: What is special about YBCO's critical temperature of 92 K?
quiz.a: It is above the boiling point of liquid nitrogen

entries.name: Inorganic acid–base chemistry
entries.tagline: Trends in the strength of acids across the periodic table, and acids stronger than water allows.

points: Down a group, acidity increases because the H–X bond gets weaker: HF (pKa 3.2) < HCl (−7) < HBr (−9) < HI (−10).
Across a period, acidity increases with the electronegativity of X: CH₄ < NH₃ < H₂O < HF.

sections.text: For an acid of the form (HO)ₘXOₚ, the pKa is roughly 8 − 5p, where p is the number of oxygen atoms without a hydrogen (the oxo groups).
facts: pKa about 8 or more. HOCl (7.5), B(OH)₃.

sections.text: Metal ions in water act as acids because the coordinated water is polarized: [M(H₂O)ₙ]^z+ ⇌ [M(H₂O)ₙ₋₁(OH)]^(z−1)+ + H⁺. Acidity rises with charge and falls with size: [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ has pKa about 2.2, [Al(H₂O)₆]³⁺ about 5, and Na⁺ essentially none. This is why salts of highly charged ions give acidic solutions.

In water, no acid can be stronger than H₃O⁺, as stronger acids simply protonate water. This is the leveling effect. To measure or use stronger acids, other solvents are used. A superacid is more acidic than 100% sulfuric acid. Magic acid, HSO₃F with SbF₅, has a Hammett acidity of about −25 and protonates even alkanes. George Olah studied carbocations in superacids and won the 1994 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

quiz.q: According to Pauling's rules, which acid is the strongest?
Why does a solution of Fe³⁺ salts have an acidic pH?
quiz.a: Coordinated water is polarized and loses H⁺ readily

entries.name: Latimer, Frost and Pourbaix diagrams
entries.tagline: Three ways to draw the redox chemistry of an element on one page.

sections.text: The species are listed in order of oxidation state, with the standard reduction potential written over the arrow between each pair. A species disproportionates if the potential on its right is more positive than the one on its left.
points: Copper in acid: Cu²⁺ →(+0.153 V) Cu⁺ →(+0.521 V) Cu. Since 0.521 > 0.153, Cu⁺ disproportionates: 2Cu⁺ → Cu²⁺ + Cu, with E° = 0.521 − 0.153 = +0.37 V. So Cu(I) is not stable in water unless it is stabilized by a ligand.
The potential for a non-adjacent step is the weighted average of those in between, weighted by electrons: E° = (n₁E₁ + n₂E₂) ÷ (n₁ + n₂).

sections.text: Plots nE° (equivalent to free energy) against oxidation number. The slope of a line between two species is the potential of that couple. Reading it:
points: Species lower on the plot are thermodynamically more stable.
A species above the line joining its two neighbors is unstable to disproportionation.
A species below it is stable, and two neighbors will comproportionate to give it.
A steep positive slope marks a strong oxidizing agent, such as permanganate.

sections.text: Plots potential E against pH and shows the region where each species is the most stable form. Two sloping lines show the limits of the stability of water, where it is oxidized to O₂ or reduced to H₂. These diagrams are used in corrosion, geochemistry and water treatment, to predict whether a metal will corrode, passivate (form a protective oxide), or stay immune. For iron, the regions are Fe, Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺, Fe(OH)₃ and so on.

quiz.q: A species disproportionates if the potential to its right on the Latimer diagram is…
quiz.a: More positive than the one to its left
wrong: More negative than the one to its left
Equal to the one to its left

entries.name: Bioinorganic chemistry
entries.tagline: How living things use metals to carry oxygen, move electrons and fix nitrogen.

points: Hemoglobin (four subunits) and myoglobin (one) hold iron(II) in a heme group, a porphyrin ring, with a histidine bound to the iron on one side. Oxygen binds on the other side.

Deoxy iron is high-spin d⁶ and sits a little out of the ring plane. When O₂ binds, the iron becomes low-spin and moves into the plane, pulling the histidine and moving the protein. This changes the other subunits, so that they bind O₂ more readily. That is cooperativity, and it gives the S-shaped oxygen binding curve that makes hemoglobin efficient at loading in the lungs and unloading in tissue.
Carbon monoxide binds to heme about 200–250 times more strongly than O₂, which is why it is poisonous.

sections.text: Cytochromes use the Fe(II)/Fe(III) couple in a heme. Iron–sulfur clusters (Fe₂S₂, Fe₄S₄) in ferredoxins carry electrons in photosynthesis and respiration. Blue copper proteins such as plastocyanin also transfer electrons.

points: Carbonic anhydrase: a zinc ion held by three histidines and a water molecule. The Zn²⁺ makes the water more acidic, producing Zn–OH, which attacks CO₂ to give hydrogen carbonate. It is one of the fastest enzymes, with about 10⁶ turnovers per second.

Nitrogenase: an iron–molybdenum cofactor reduces N₂ to NH₃ at room temperature and pressure: N₂ + 8H⁺ + 8e⁻ + 16 ATP → 2NH₃ + H₂ + 16 ADP + 16 Pᵢ. It contrasts with the high temperature and pressure of the Haber–Bosch process.
Vitamin B₁₂ has cobalt in a corrin ring, with a Co–C bond, rare in biology.

sections.text: Chlorophyll is a magnesium complex of a porphyrin-like ring. Mg²⁺ keeps the ring rigid and the excited states long-lived.

Essential trace metals include Fe, Zn, Cu, Mn, Co, Mo. Too much or too little causes disease. Chelating agents such as EDTA remove toxic metals. Cisplatin is a Pt anticancer drug, and gold compounds have been used for arthritis.

quiz.q: What metal is at the center of heme in hemoglobin?
What is cooperativity in hemoglobin?
quiz.a: Binding of O₂ to one subunit makes the others bind it more easily
wrong: Four O₂ bind at one iron

entries.name: Lanthanides and actinides
entries.tagline: The f-block: very similar chemistry across a row, and some of the most useful materials.

points: The 4f orbitals are buried deep inside the atom, so they take little part in bonding. The lanthanides are therefore chemically very similar, almost always +3, and form ionic compounds.

The lanthanide contraction: as 4f electrons are added across the row, they shield the nuclear charge poorly, so the ionic radius falls steadily, from 103 pm for La³⁺ to 86 pm for Lu³⁺. A consequence is that the 5d elements follow the 4d elements with almost the same size: Zr (160 pm) and Hf (159 pm) are almost identical chemically and very hard to separate.
Exceptions to +3: Ce⁴⁺ (f⁰) and Eu²⁺ (f⁷) are stable because of the empty and half-filled shell.
The f–f transitions are sharp and weak, since the 4f orbitals are shielded and the transitions are Laporte forbidden. So the colors are pale and the excited states long-lived.
Europium and terbium in phosphors for lighting and screens (Eu³⁺ is red). Neodymium in Nd:YAG lasers (1064 nm), erbium in optical fiber amplifiers.
Strong magnets: Nd₂Fe₁₄B and SmCo₅.
Separation is hard, because of the similar sizes. It is done by repeated ion-exchange or solvent extraction.

sections.text: All are radioactive. The 5f orbitals extend further than the 4f, so they take more part in bonding, and the early actinides show a range of oxidation states: uranium +3 to +6 (the uranyl ion, UO₂²⁺, is the common form in solution) and plutonium +3 to +7. Later actinides behave more like lanthanides, mainly +3.

quiz.q: What is the lanthanide contraction?
quiz.a: A steady decrease in ionic radius across the lanthanide series
wrong: An increase in radius across the series

quiz.q: Why are Zr and Hf so chemically similar?
quiz.a: The lanthanide contraction makes them almost the same size
wrong: They have the same number of protons
They are in the same period

entries.name: Characterization of inorganic compounds
entries.tagline: The methods that tell you what you have made.

facts: The most complete answer: the 3D structure with bond lengths and angles. Needs a good crystal.
Identifies crystalline phases by comparing with databases, and checks purity. The Scherrer equation, D = Kλ ÷ (β cos θ), estimates the size of nanocrystals from peak broadening.
Ligand vibrations (ν(CO), ν(NO), ν(CN)), and metal–ligand stretches at low frequency.
d–d and charge-transfer bands, giving Δₒ, geometry and oxidation state.
Diamagnetic complexes. ³¹P NMR of phosphine complexes is very informative. Paramagnetic complexes have broad, shifted signals.

Detects unpaired electrons. The g value (2.0023 for a free electron) and hyperfine splitting from nuclear spins show the electronic structure and the metal environment. For Cu²⁺ in an elongated octahedron, g‖ > g⊥.

For ⁵⁷Fe (and ¹¹⁹Sn): the isomer shift and quadrupole splitting identify the oxidation and spin state. High-spin Fe(II) has an isomer shift of about 1.0–1.3 mm/s and large splitting, and Fe(III) about 0.3–0.5 mm/s.
Redox potentials, and how reversible the electron transfer is.
Oxidation state and local structure, even in non-crystalline samples.
CHN analysis gives the composition, within about 0.4%. ESI-MS shows the mass of ionic complexes.

sections.text: No single method is enough. A new compound is usually characterized by several of them, which together confirm the formula, the structure and the electronic state.

quiz.q: Which technique detects unpaired electrons directly?
